chief_complaint: sudden pounding headache, severe hypertension 210/115, sweating above chest, and nasal congestion in T4 spinal cord injury (Autonomic Dysreflexia)
hpi_details: 28M with chronic complete T4 paraplegia from a motor vehicle crash 3 years ago presents to urgent rehabilitation clinic with sudden onset of a violent, pounding headache, profuse drenching sweating across his face, neck, and shoulders, flushing of his upper chest, and severe nasal congestion. He reports feeling intensely anxious and flushed above his chest, while his legs feel cold and clammy below the waist.
ideas: in severe distress holding his head, terrified he is having a stroke
concerns: knows his blood pressure is dangerously high right now
expectations: wants immediate check of his urinary catheter and emergency blood pressure lowering
pmh: Complete T4 spinal cord injury (ASIA Grade A), Neurogenic bladder on suprapubic catheter

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Autonomic Dysreflexia is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes immediate positioning, removal of the noxious stimulus, and short-acting antihypertensive therapy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden pounding headache, severe hypertension 210/115, sweating above chest, and nasal congestion in T4 spinal cord injury (Autonomic Dysreflexia)

Key HPI features: 28M with chronic complete T4 paraplegia from a motor vehicle crash 3 years ago presents to urgent rehabilitation clinic with sudden onset of a violent, pounding headache, profuse drenching sweating across his face, neck, and shoulders, flushing of his upper chest, and severe nasal congestion. He reports feeling intensely anxious and flushed above his chest, while his legs feel cold and clammy below the waist.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: BP 212/114 (baseline resting BP in high SCI patients is typically low around 90-100/60 mmHg, representing a catastrophic increase >100 mmHg), HR 48 (reflex bradycardia triggered by carotid baroreceptor stimulation), Temp 36.9C. Physical exam reveals marked erythema, flushing, and hyperhidrosis over the face, neck, and upper thorax (above the T4 lesion level), contrasted with pale, cool, cutis anserina (goosebumps) skin over the lower extremities (below the lesion level). Inspection of his suprapubic urinary catheter reveals the drainage tubing is kinked under his wheelchair cushion and the bladder is palpably distended and tense.
Relevant background/PMH: Complete T4 spinal cord injury (ASIA Grade A), Neurogenic bladder on suprapubic catheter
Current medications: Baclofen 20mg TID, Oxybutynin 5mg BID
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Autonomic Dysreflexia.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Hypertensive crisis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Systolic BP > 200 mmHg.
management_principles: STAT PM&R emergency step-by-step protocol: identify and remove the inciting noxious stimulus while positioning the patient and controlling blood pressure.
Immediately sit the patient upright at 90 degrees and drop the legs (taking advantage of orthostatic pooling to lower intracranial and arterial blood pressure)
Loosen all restrictive clothing, abdominal binders, and compression stockings immediately
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 28M with chronic high thoracic (T4) complete spinal cord injury presenting with acute pounding headache, upper body diaphoresis/flushing, and severe hypertension, classic for Autonomic Dysreflexia.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 212/114 (baseline resting BP in high SCI patients is typically low around 90-100/60 mmHg, representing a catastrophic increase >100 mmHg), HR 48 (reflex bradycardia triggered by carotid baroreceptor stimulation), Temp 36.9C. Physical exam reveals marked erythema, flushing, and hyperhidrosis over the face, neck, and upper thorax (above the T4 lesion level), contrasted with pale, cool, cutis anserina (goosebumps) skin over the lower extremities (below the lesion level). Inspection of his suprapubic urinary catheter reveals the drainage tubing is kinked under his wheelchair cushion and the bladder is palpably distended and tense.
reference_soap.assessment: Medical Emergency: Autonomic Dysreflexia (Hyperreflexia) secondary to bladder distension in T4 complete spinal cord injury.
reference_soap.plan: Medical emergency: activate the local emergency response/transfer pathway and monitor blood pressure frequently. While awaiting emergency care, sit the patient upright with legs dependent, loosen restrictive clothing, and identify and relieve an accessible noxious stimulus such as a kinked catheter. Catheter replacement and evaluation for bowel or skin triggers require trained clinicians. If systolic blood pressure remains above 150 mmHg after these measures, a clinician may use a rapid-onset, short-duration antihypertensive under local protocol after checking contraindications, including recent phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor use.

learning_objectives: Recognize Autonomic Dysreflexia as a potentially lethal neurological emergency occurring exclusively in spinal cord injuries at or above the T6 level, triggered by noxious stimuli (bladder distension 80%, bowel impaction, skin pressure) below the lesion

Identify the classic clinical triad of Autonomic Dysreflexia: severe paroxysmal hypertension, reflex bradycardia, and differential vasomotor symptoms (flushing/sweating ABOVE the T6 lesion vs vasoconstriction/pallor/goosebumps BELOW the lesion)

Execute immediate bedside step-by-step management: sit upright at 90 degrees, loosen tight garments, and systematically inspect/drain the urinary bladder or relieve bowel impaction using anesthetic jelly

Select an appropriate rapidly reversible short-acting antihypertensive, such as topical nitroglycerin ointment after screening for recent phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor use, when blood pressure remains dangerously elevated despite mechanical stimulus removal

teaching.one_liner: Potentially life-threatening hypertensive emergency in spinal cord injury at or above T6, triggered by noxious stimuli below the lesion level.

must_ask.say: What is the level of your spinal cord injury?
Is your urinary catheter draining properly, or could it be blocked or kinked?
When was your last bowel movement, and do you feel constipated?
Is this headache sudden and pounding in nature?
Are you sweating or flushing above your spinal injury while feeling cold below it?

history.answer: Doctor, my head is pounding violently like it is about to explode, and I am sweating like crazy all over my chest.
It started out of nowhere about thirty minutes ago, and within just a couple of minutes it peaked into the worst pounding pain I have ever felt.
The pounding has been relentless and nonstop for the past thirty minutes. I have never had a headache anywhere near this severe in my life.
It is throbbing all over my head, but the pressure feels especially violent right behind my eyes, at both temples, and in the back of my skull.
It is a severe, violent throbbing that hammers with every single heartbeat. On a scale of one to ten, it is easily a ten.
It hit me suddenly while I was sitting in my wheelchair this morning, and it has stayed at the same agonizing intensity the entire time.
If I lean back or try to lie flat, the pounding becomes unbearable, so sitting upright is the only way I can tolerate it at all.
No, I did not have any warning signs like flashing lights, zigzag lines, or blind spots before the headache struck.
I feel nauseous just from how intense the pounding is, but I haven't thrown up. Light and loud sounds do not make it worse.
Both sides of my nose suddenly became completely stuffed up, though my eyes are not tearing and my eyelids are not drooping.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or neck stiffness, and there is no rash on my skin.
My arms move completely fine and my speech is clear, though I have been paralyzed from my chest down since my car accident three years ago.
My vision is a little blurry from the sheer pressure pounding in my head, but I don't have double vision or pain inside my eyeballs.
No, I have not bumped my head, fallen, or had any kind of injury recently.
I almost never take painkillers, and I haven't taken any pills or pain medicine today.
No, I slept well, haven't been under unusual stress, and haven't had alcohol, caffeine, or aged foods.
My resting blood pressure is usually very low, around ninety over sixty, so I don't take blood pressure medications or blood thinners.
No one else around me has a headache or feels sick, and our heaters are working properly.
No, I have never had cancer, HIV, or taken any immune-suppressing medications.
I suffered a complete T4 spinal cord injury from a car crash three years ago, leaving me paralyzed and without feeling below my mid-chest.
I have a suprapubic catheter tube into my bladder, but my lower belly feels tight and swollen, and no urine has entered the bag for hours.
I follow a bowel program every other morning with suppositories, had a normal bowel movement yesterday, and have not had constipation.
I am drenched in sweat and flushed red across my face, neck, and chest, but my legs below my waist feel icy cold with goosebumps.
I know my blood pressure must be dangerously high right now, and I am terrified that this pounding headache means I am having a stroke.
Please check my urinary catheter immediately to see if it is blocked or kinked, and help lower my blood pressure before something bursts.
Apart from my spinal cord injury, paralyzed bladder, and muscle spasms, I do not have other medical conditions.
I had spine stabilization surgery, suprapubic tube placement, and extensive inpatient rehabilitation after my crash three years ago.
I take baclofen twenty milligrams three times daily for muscle spasms, and oxybutynin five milligrams twice daily for bladder spasms.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
No, I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I do not drink alcohol.
I used to work as a carpenter before my accident, and now I live in a wheelchair-accessible apartment with part-time helper support.
There is no family history of high blood pressure, aneurysms, migraines, or early strokes.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 212/114 mmHg, heart rate is 48 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, and body temperature is 36.9 degrees Celsius.
The patient is in acute, severe distress sitting in a wheelchair, holding his head, with profuse sweating and flushing over the face, neck, and upper chest.
Marked erythema, flushing, and heavy diaphoresis are present above the T4 level, whereas the lower extremities below T4 are pale, cool to the touch, and exhibit prominent goosebumps.
Pupils are equal, round, and briskly reactive to light; fundoscopic examination reveals sharp optic disc margins without papilledema or retinal hemorrhages.
There is no tenderness over the frontal or maxillary sinuses, and no tenderness or thickening over either temporal artery.
Nasal mucosal membranes are markedly engorged and edematous bilaterally without discharge; oropharynx is clear without mucosal lesions.
The neck is completely supple with full range of motion, and both Kernig and Brudzinski signs are negative.
Cranial nerves II through XII are fully intact, with symmetric facial movements and clear, articulate speech.
Upper extremity muscle strength is 5/5 bilaterally, while lower extremities exhibit 0/5 flaccid paralysis consistent with chronic complete paraplegia.
Light touch and pinprick sensation are completely preserved above the T4 dermatome, with complete sensory loss below the nipple line.
A suprapubic catheter is in place with the drainage tubing sharply kinked underneath the wheelchair cushion, preventing any urine outflow into the drainage bag.
The suprapubic region is visibly tense and firmly distended from acute urinary retention, while the rest of the abdomen is soft and non-tender without organomegaly.
